en: Ji'en Zhengyi: Now, one who leaves the household life does so out of weariness with worldly toil and the desire to seek liberation from birth and death; by ceasing the mind and quieting thoughts, they sever all攀缘 (pān-yuán, clinging/dependencies).
This is why it is called "leaving the household. How can one allow ordinary gain and sustenance to bury one's entire life? One must simply cast both ends aside.
Open it. Let go in the middle. Encountering sounds or forms is like planting flowers upon a stone; seeing profit or fame is like having grit in one’s eye.
Moreover, from time immemorial, there is nothing you have not already experienced, nor is there anything you do not know in its proper sequence.
It is merely that you turn the beginning into the end, stopping at this very point. Why must you cling so desperately? Now, at this moment—
Do not rest. When else would you wait? Therefore, when the ancient sages taught people, they simply wanted them to exhaust this present moment.
Once you can exhaust this present moment, what further matter could there be? If you attain a state where the mind is free from affairs, even Buddhas and Patriarchs are but enemies;
all worldly matters naturally become indifferent, and only then will you correspond with that "other side. Have you not seen how Yinyangshan lived until his death [without leaving]?
He was willing to see people. Zhaozhou, until the end of his life, never told anyone [of his realization]. Biandan gathered acorns and chestnuts for food;
Damei used lotus leaves as clothing; Zhidaoshi wore only paper; and the Venerable Xuantai wore only cloth.
Shishuang established the "Hall of Withered Trees" where he lay down with the assembly, desiring only to kill your mind. Touzi sent someone to prepare [his funeral].
Cooking rice together and eating it as one is intended to save you effort; moreover, the various sages of antiquity have set such an example.
If there were no merit in this, how could one bear it? O virtuous ones, if you investigate this thoroughly, you will certainly not fail others;
if you are unwilling to take it up, I fear you will find it difficult in the future. This mountain monk’s own practice is not worth taking as a model.
Having the honor of presiding over this mountain gate, how could I sit idly while consuming the communal property (changzhu) and utterly forget the final instructions of the former sages?

Now, I intend to briefly emulate the ancient masters in establishing the protocols for a *zhuchi* (abbot). I have deliberated with all of you and resolved that I shall no longer descend the mountain, nor attend formal meals, nor dispatch emissaries to solicit alms;
instead, I shall take the annual yield from the monastery’s estates and divide it into three hundred and sixty equal portions.
It is sufficient to take one portion each day; do not increase or decrease it according to others. If there is enough for a full meal, prepare a meal;
if insufficient for a meal, prepare gruel; if insufficient for gruel, prepare rice broth. For newly arrived guests, provide only tea and soup upon meeting;
do not further boil or prepare other items. Establish only a single tea hall where individuals may go to fetch and use what they need, with the aim of practicing frugality.

With single-minded focus, one discerns the Way; how much more so when one’s livelihood is complete and the scenery is never neglected? Flowers understand how to smile, and birds understand how to sing;
wooden horses neigh long, and stone oxen run well. Beyond the heavens, the green mountains lack their colors;
by one’s ears, the murmuring springs have no sound. On the ridges above, monkeys cry as the dew wets the moon at midnight; within the forests, cranes call as the wind returns the clarity.
The pines of dawn: when the spring breeze arises, the withered trees roar like dragons; when the autumn leaves fall, the flowers of the cold forest scatter.
Upon the jade steps, patterns of moss and lichen are spread; human faces bear the hues of mist and clouds. Sounds and traces are silent, yet the message remains perfectly intact.
All is a single flavor of desolation, with nowhere to turn. Today, this mountain monk speaks of the home before you all.

Since you have already failed to avoid this pitfall at the gate, how could you go further to ascend the hall and enter the room, wielding the mallet and brandishing the whisk, shouting to the east and striking with the staff to the west, knitting your brows and glaring with eyes wide as if a seizure had broken out?

This not only causes the Venerable One to sink into obscurity, but moreover, it betrays the ancient sages. Have you not seen how Bodhidharma came from the West to Mount Shaoshi and sat facing a wall for nine years? II.
The Patriarch went so far as to stand in the snow and cut off his own arm; one could say he underwent every hardship imaginable.
Yet, Dharma never uttered a single word, and the Second Patriarch never asked a single question. Can you call Dharma "one who does not act for others"?
Can you call the Second Patriarch "one who does not seek a teacher"? Whenever I speak of the deeds of these ancient sages, [I find them truly wondrous].
One suddenly feels there is no ground upon which to stand, filled with shame for one's own weakness.

How much more so when others provide one with the finest delicacies of a hundred flavors in succession, saying, "Only when you are fully provided with the four requisites can you resolve to cultivate the Way.
Fearing that one’s efforts will not suffice, one may find oneself separated by lifetimes or even eons. Time passes like a flying arrow; it is truly a great pity. Nevertheless, even so, furthermore—
As for judging others by their physical appearance, even I, this mountain monk, cannot force you to understand it. Gentlemen, do you see the verse of the ancients?
"Rice from the mountain fields, coarse; wild vegetables with plain yellow pickles. Eat them if you wish; if not, go as you please.
I humbly entreat you, my fellow practitioners: each of you must exert yourselves. Take care.
Engraved on bamboo: The Dharma Words of the Patriarch Fuyong Kai.

Alas! Many of us late-born disciples are day and night busily preoccupied with the worry that our wealth and honor do not suffice for ourselves, or that our fame and reputation are not manifest in the world.
Although we outwardly engage in meditation and recitation, merely feigning their appearance...
Regarding monastic decorum: within the inner circle, one should entirely cast aside one's own great affairs beyond the bounds of concern, remaining tranquil and unaware of oneself.
If one daily opens and recites these strict instructions of the ancestral master Yongping Kai, and thereby feels a sense of shame, then one may perhaps reach the state of tireless diligence.
This advancement in study will surely assist the stage of the spiritual ground (*bhūmi*). I rejoice that he has now devised this medicinal broth to prolong life;
his diligence in carving and circulating this work is truly praiseworthy. Therefore, I have composed these words to express my old heart’s sympathetic joy.
In the second month of spring in the Renzi year of the Kōsei era,
the distant descendant, the aged bhikṣu of Kūge-an, Gentō, respectfully wrote this with a pure mind.
